payload.rationale: I estimate a 15% chance that the contract-defined CDC count of U.S. measles cases in 2026 exceeds 6,000. Historical background favors NO: post-elimination annual U.S. totals have generally been far below this threshold; the substantial 2019 outbreak year recorded approximately 1,300 cases. However, measles is exceptionally contagious, and concentrated immunity gaps can support large, sustained outbreaks. My estimate assumes that this outbreak risk warrants a meaningful upper tail beyond the historical baseline; it is not based on observed 2026 case counts. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that vaccination, outbreak containment, and geographically limited transmission may keep national totals well below 6,001. The strongest reason it could be too low is that declining coverage and connected undervaccinated communities could already have produced extensive transmission in 2026, which the empty evidence packet would not reveal. I do not interpret the absence of supplied reports as evidence of low incidence. Settlement depends on the CDC count accepted under the frozen rules, excluding revisions after expiration, rather than an unrestricted eventual total.
limitations: No 2026 year-to-date case count, outbreak trajectory, or current vaccination evidence was supplied, despite the September 19 forecast cutoff.
The probability is a subjective historical-base-rate and outbreak-risk judgment, not a fitted or currently calibrated epidemiological forecast.
CDC reporting timing and the exclusion of post-expiration revisions could affect settlement near the threshold.
